en: The Śramaṇa Jì composed this commentary on the *Sūtra* passage: "The bhikṣus entered deeply into meditative concentration. The eulogy states: The preceding section explains past causes, intending to cause those who would regress from the Great [Vehicle] to turn toward the Small;
the following section reveals the present fruit, intending to cause them to know how to relinquish the provisional in order to...
The actual meaning is taken up.
The text is divided into three parts:
first, the principle (*dharma*); second, the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*); and third, the application (*upanaya*). Therefore.
The initial section has two parts:
first, clarifying the present reality; second, explaining the reasons for the prior provisional teachings, which begins with the words, "Bhikṣus, you should know.
This first part further consists of two sections:
First, one knows that the faculties are matured, and subsequently teaches the One Vehicle.
This refers to the first [stage].
There are five ways in which the faculties become matured:
First, the time for his parinirvāṇa has arrived;
the faculties of sentient beings have matured, and he fears that if they hear of his nirvāṇa immediately, they will believe it with excessive depth.
Second, the assembly is also pure.
Because their afflictions have become slight and they gradually depart from defilement;

whereas it was previously taught that the Three Vehicles emerge in a turbid age when sentient beings' impurities are heavy, now, having transformed them for a long time, they are gradually led to leave behind these impurities, and are therefore called "pure."
Third, firmness in resolute belief:
both realization-understanding and realized-belief are firm and cannot be obstructed or destroyed.
Fourth, thorough comprehension of the dharma of emptiness.
There are two kinds of emptiness: first, the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā), and second, the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā).

The emptiness of persons is that which is realized, while the emptiness of phenomena is that which is known; this is because, after having already realized the emptiness of persons, one hears the Prajñāpāramitā and thereby comes to know the emptiness of phenomena.
Fifth, they deeply enter meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Because they are able to enter and emerge from the four *dhyānas* and nine concentrations, this is explained in reference to those śrāvakas who, having regressed, once again give rise to the great mind (*mahācitta*).
Only when these five [qualities] are fully possessed do they realize the two provisional [means] and return to the one reality; otherwise, it is not so.
The Sūtra says: "He then assembled all the bodhisattvas until they attained parinirvāṇa.
The commentary states:
This explains the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
Since it has been taught that the four [yānas] constitute the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), while the teaching of one [yāna] is a provisional means (*upāya*).
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"I have already revealed that the nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the nature of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) are all without intrinsic nature."
"If one does not understand this intentional meaning (*saṃdhi*) of the Buddha, one will lose the right path and be unable to proceed.
Within this context, the establishment of a single vehicle (*ekayāna*) is not because there is no distinction in the nature (*gotra*) of sentient beings.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* also states:

"Sons of good family who embrace the true Dharma are capable of bearing four kinds of heavy responsibilities that surpass even the great earth; namely, they bring to maturity through the roots of goodness of humans and devas those sentient beings who lack learning and follow what is not the Dharma."
This refers to the "small grasses" mentioned among the three types.
Those who seek the state of a śrāvaka are given the Śrāvaka-yāna, and those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha are given the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; these together constitute the small grasses.
To those who seek the Mahāyāna, one bestows the Mahāyāna; this is precisely the "great grass.
Furthermore, it is said: "If the Tathāgata teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations, there is only the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and no other vehicles."
Thus we know that, according to the underlying principle, teaching [the Buddha-nature] as one is provisional, while teaching it as four is ultimate.
The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "It is not because the nature of sentient beings lacks differentiation."
In this sutra, in order to transform those who have regressed and cause them to again resolve upon the Great Mind, it is said that the One is real while the Two are expedient.

Only when their faculties have matured and the five conditions are fully met is it taught that there are no two vehicles by which one attains extinction; rather, it is solely through the Buddha Vehicle that one attains extinction.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is stated that all śrāvakas will either attain Buddhahood or not attain Buddhahood;
the World-Honored One declared that both [views] fail to understand my intention.
Therefore, being able to understand the intent of the sutra in this way, one should also skillfully accord with the minds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
However, as most in this assembly have regressed in their nature, it is said that while the One Reality is ultimate, the two [vehicles] are expedient.
The Sūtra says: "Bhikṣus, you should know that upon arrival, they will immediately believe and accept [it].
The commentary states:
This explains the reasons for the prior use of provisional means (*upāya*).

By means of the wisdom of skillful means, I realize the faculties, natures, and inclinations of sentient beings; seeing that their aspirations are small and they are fundamentally attached to the five desires, I grant them minor teachings so that they may abandon those five desires and extricate themselves from the suffering of birth and death.
The five desires are precisely the craving for the five objects; therefore, [the Buddha] first spoke of nirvāṇa and established the city of transformation to provide rest from suffering.
Once they have attained nirvāṇa, if these people hear that the One Vehicle is now being taught to lead them to the place of treasure, they will immediately believe and accept it.
The Sūtra says: "It is, for example, like five hundred [people] reaching a place of rare treasures.
The Commentary states: This is the explanation by means of a secondary analogy.
This section contains two parts:
first, a metaphor for the provisional [teachings] of the past;
second, a metaphor for the ultimate reality of the present, which begins with the passage: "At that time, the guide knew that this multitude of people... and so forth.
The initial text consists of four parts:

first, the metaphor of being about to leave the perilous place; second, from "the multitude of people being led" onwards, the metaphor of withdrawing midway; third, from "the guide possesses many skillful means" onwards, the metaphor of establishing a conjured city; and fourth, from "at that time, the exhausted multitude" onwards, the metaphor of the weary assembly finally coming to rest.
In the previous "Chapter on Resolute Belief," there were six metaphors for the provisional [teachings] of the past; these current ones are identical to those, yet they lack the first two.

This is because at the time of the initial regression, one had not yet turned toward the Lesser Vehicle, nor had the "transformed city" been established; therefore, they are omitted here, and only the latter four are shared.
Alternatively, this first [analogy] regarding the initial departure from danger subsumes both the first and third [analogies] of that [text];

the second here subsumes both the second and fourth there; and these latter two analogies here subsume the latter two there. Although there are differences in their expansion and contraction, there is no distinction in their meaning.
The initial analogy has four parts:

first, the fault of desiring a dangerous place; second, setting out for the direction of the treasure; third, the merchant leader’s familiarity with the route; and fourth, leading the way during the journey.
This refers to the first two.
Regarding "five hundred *yojanas*," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The cycle of birth and death within the five destinies is called a perilous and evil path.
"Vast" (*kuang*) means empty, sparse, long-lasting, and distant.
"Isolated" (*jue*) means remote.
Within the cycle of birth and death, there is fundamentally no sage or wise person; it is like a vast, desolate void, remote and devoid of people—this is truly something to be deeply alarmed by.
The phrase "the five fears and so forth" refers to the objects of fear.
Now, to provide another interpretation: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reveals the nature of the perilous path; it does not merely explain their numerical count.

Regarding the statement "five hundred": within *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth-and-death), there are three hundred [yojanas] consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*); within *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth-and-death), there are two hundred consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) and suffering. Because the ten categories of fruits induced by the ten afflictions and ten paths of karma mutually support one another, they are combined and termed "five hundred. The subsequent mention of "more than three hundred yojanas" refers to the establishment of the *nirmāṇa-pura* (the conjured city).

If one were to count based on the five destinies, the number would be five; however, since those who have passed beyond the three evil destinies have only begun to enter the vision of the truths (darśana-mārga) and have not yet seen the illusory city (nirvāṇa), how could they be said to have "entered"?
Therefore, one should rely on the latter explanation.
"The place of rare treasures" refers to the stage of the fruit of Buddhahood in the Great Parinirvāṇa; it is a metaphor for transcending the perils of saṃsāra only to reach the state of Buddhahood.
As the Sūtra says: "There was a guide who intended to pass beyond this difficulty."
The commentary states:
Within this there are two parts;
first, the merchant leader, being conversant with the routes, proceeds to provide guidance.
"Guide" refers to the Buddha, who possesses five virtues: first, the nature of intelligence due to sharp faculties;

second, the wisdom that discriminates between right and wrong; third, the clear illumination of both the ultimate and conventional truths; fourth, the thorough penetration of all things such that nothing remains unknown; and fifth, the skillful knowledge of the characteristics of dangerous paths, whether they are passable or obstructed.
"Path" refers to the various realms of existence;
"openness" refers to severing the five stages of dwelling;
"obstruction" refers to giving rise to the two hindrances.
Delusion and karma exist as obstructions, while the exhaustion of the causes of suffering constitutes the path.
As for the guidance provided during the journey, the meaning of the text is clear.
The Sūtra states: "The multitude of people being led now wish to turn back."
The commentary states:
This is the second analogy, that of retreating midway.
Having cultivated the causes of the Mahāyāna for less than sixty kalpas, one becomes weary of practicing the bodhisattva path; this is termed "fatigue and indolence on the way."
The great practices are difficult to cultivate and involve enduring every kind of hardship; this is called "exhaustion.
Because the duration of such weariness is long, it is further termed "extreme exhaustion.
To fear the ocean of noble conduct and to be timid regarding progress in cultivation is likewise called "dread."
Because they are terrified by the greatness of the practice, they are called "those who fear.
Unable to advance toward the fruit of great enlightenment, the path before them remains long even after three great eons.
To retreat from the Great Vehicle, failing to study and instead remaining within saṃsāra, is called "retreating now."
This is an explanation according to the meaning;
it is not that the two vehicles actually requested permission from the Buddha in the past and subsequently regressed to abide in the Lesser Vehicle.
As the Sūtra says: "The Guide employs many skillful means, even to the point of conjuring a city."
The commentary states:
The following third section provides the parable of the conjured city.
It consists of four parts:
First, the provisional contemplation; second, the establishment of the conjured city; third, the exhortation to remain without fear; and fourth, the explanation of the benefits of entering the city.
These are the first two [of the four].
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:

"Just as the wish-fulfilling jewel and the celestial drum accomplish their own tasks without volition, so too, although there is no effortful volition, there is spontaneous volition; for although there is no actual volition, it is metaphorically designated as 'volition'."
The Buddhas constantly survey sentient beings six times throughout the day and night; this is because their activity is like that of intentional thought.

Regarding the phrase "beyond three hundred yojanas": if one says the five destinies constitute five hundred [yojanas], this refers to transcending the birth-and-death of the segmented realm (*prādeśika-saṃsāra*) and emerging from the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Alternatively, it may be said that they cause one to emerge forever from the three evil destinies; thus, there are three [fetters], because the three beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) among the five lower fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are mentioned later, while in reality, they have already been severed at the outset.

Although the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) death-and-rebirth also issues from the realms of humans and devas, the *pariṇāmi-vaśitā* (transformative) death-and-rebirth is still subsumed under the destinies of humans and devas; therefore, it is not called "transcending.

According to the correct teaching, the *paricchinna-bheda* death-and-rebirth consists of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*); because [the transformative] is free from these three, it is said to be "beyond three hundred yojanas."
Because *nirvāṇa* resides in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Regarding "transforming it into a city," the *Mūla-śāstra* states: "The cities of the various *dhyānas* and *samādhis*—having passed beyond those cities, one causes entry into the city of Great *Nirvāṇa*. Therefore, the Buddha spoke of 'provisional establishment' (*prajñapti*); because there is no substantial reality, he said it was 'transformed.'"

He realizes the meditative concentration associated with the cessation of the mind, which, together with pliancy and bliss, is able to pacify the heavy and coarse elements; thus, the Buddha’s teaching is termed "transformation.
Since the principle of cessation is non-dual, it is called "one" in contrast to the vehicle of the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, although these are conventional designations, individuals differ from one another; yet, because their conventional meaning is the same, they are called "one.
Moreover, because the capacities and the studies of those who realize the Two Vehicles differ, the subsequent verse states: "Because it is a place of rest, two are taught."
Using the provisional to contrast with the real: since the real is non-dual, how could the provisional not be non-one?
This illustrates *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Because delusions and karma have been severed, suffering no longer arises; thus, one truly attains *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
The wisdom of the remaining bodies is termed "non-attainment" (aprāpti) as long as it has not yet been realized; only when the wisdom of the final body perishes is it termed "realization" (prāpti).
This is like the unconditioned state of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*), which is described according to its ultimate fulfillment.
The Sūtra says, “He addressed the multitude, saying... until ‘you may also depart.
The Commentary states:
Within this passage there are two parts.
He exhorts him to remain steadfast and not fear;
he explains the benefits of entering the city with the passage beginning, "If one enters this city.

One need not fear that it is too great and thus refuse to practice; rather, enter this city and act as you please, practicing according to your capacity so that the true intent may be manifested through rest.
There are two benefits to skillfully establishing provisional means:
first, one attains peaceful stability and brings rest to manifold sufferings; second, after heading toward the stage of Buddhahood, one can gradually engage in cultivation.
As the sutra states: "At that time, the exhausted multitude conceived the thought of having attained peace and security."
The commentary says:
This fourth section provides analogies for the exhaustion and cessation of all weariness.
It consists of two parts:
Initially, while still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), one is called "joyful in mind," speaking with praise of a joyful heart and intending to escape the perilous path;

later, having attained the stage of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one enters the "transformed city" (*nirmāṇa-pura*). Having attained cessation with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirodha*), one gives rise to the thought that birth has already been transcended. Because one has transcended birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and abandoned suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*), yet because the death-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāma-cyuti*) has not yet truly been left behind, one gives rise to the thought that birth has been transcended and the thought of peace and security.

Because one has attained no-more-learning and realized cessation and the path, yet has not yet attained the true peace and security of Great Nirvāṇa (*mahā-parinirvāṇa*), one gives rise to the thought of peace and security, and subsequently generates the four kinds of wisdom:
"My births have been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:

"Because an arhat does not accomplish all immeasurable and equal merits, it is said that they have attained nirvāṇa"; it further states: "The claim that one attains a place of ultimate rest through the four knowledges is the Buddha’s skillful means, an incomplete teaching of provisional meaning."
Therefore, this "transformed city" (nirvāṇa) is a provisional device established by the Buddha.

When one correctly gives rise to the wisdom of the emptiness of birth and realizes the principle of the emptiness of birth, such that subsequent afflictions no longer arise, this is called "entering the city.

At that time, these two notions do not exist; it is only later, upon entering a conventional meditative absorption and retrospectively observing the preceding stage, that these notions arise. Since the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is a provisional cessation, it is said that they previously entered the transformed city.

The two types of vehicle-knowledge were originally non-existent; the two sons left the house but did not board the vehicles. Since the vehicles were unattached and they sought them after leaving the house, it is said that they "entered first" because the cities were provided along the way.
All such objections have already been addressed as previously explained.
Regarding the Sūtra passage, “At that time, the Guide arrives only to bring rest,” the commentary says:
The second section below now explains the reality;
it has two parts:
first, the indication that the transformation [body] has ceased, and second, the formal proclamation of the truth.

"Extinguishing the transformation" means leading them to the Mahāyāna by explaining that the nirvāṇa of the two vehicles is a provisional analytical cessation; thus it is called "extinguishing the transformation," rather than actually extinguishing that conjured city through supernatural power.
In this context, the statement "the great city toward which we were headed was a transformation created by me" refers to the fact that the conjured city has ceased to exist.
The phrase "the place of treasure is near" indicates the reality.

Although they are those beyond training (aśaikṣa), because they cultivate the great causes through a circuitous path and their practice is slower than sudden awakening, they are even more rapid than those still in training (śaikṣa) who turn their minds [toward enlightenment]; therefore, it is said that [the goal] is near.
Regarding the sūtra passage, “The bhikṣus should go when it is time to go, and they should deliver [beings] when it is time to deliver,” the commentary states:
This is explained below in conjunction with the following.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the reconciliation with the former provisional [teachings]; second, from the passage "If sentient beings abide in the two stages" onwards, the reconciliation with the present reality.
The first section has three parts:

The first section, "When first setting out," corresponds to the initial departure from the perilous place; the next section, beginning with "If sentient beings merely hear," corresponds to turning back midway; and the final section, beginning with "The Buddha, knowing this mind," corresponds to preaching the manifestation of the *parinirvāṇa-city*.

It is not appropriate for the fourth assembly to rest their weariness, as this intends to clarify the two paths of the provisional and the ultimate, rather than specifically clarifying the cessation of suffering.
This is the first point.
"Departing" means heading toward Nirvana.
"Deliverance" (*tāraṇa*) means to transcend birth and death.
Regarding the sūtra passage, "If sentient beings [practice] until they attain it, they shall be able to achieve [it]," the commentary states:
This combination would cause them to withdraw midway.

If one were to praise only the Buddha Vehicle, sentient beings would be unable to attain deliverance through it; because they would undergo diligent suffering for a long time, they would consequently fall away. This is because the path of the Buddha is long and distant, leading to weariness over such a long duration, and because they fear the great undertaking of enduring diligent suffering for so long.
The Sūtra states: "The Buddha knows this mind... [up to] he speaks of two nirvāṇas.
The commentary says:
This section collectively explains the "transformed city" (pariṇāmika-nagara).
Because there are those who are timid toward the Mahāyāna and those of inferior capacity who delight in the Lesser Vehicle, two types of nirvāṇa are taught within the Middle Way.
These are called the two nirvāṇas because they are what is studied by these two types of practitioners and what is realized by their two corresponding wisdoms.
The essence of the two nirvāṇas is merely that one is *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder); it does not mean that *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* are themselves the two.

As for the previous statement that there is "one city," this was because the transformation [body] is one when contrasted with the True [Dharmakāya], and because there is no difference in principle when contrasted with the phenomenal principle;
now, when contrasted with the capacities of sentient beings, the causes cultivated and the wisdom realized are called the "two nirvāṇas," which is likewise not contradictory.
Regarding the sūtra passage from "If sentient beings... up to "...distinguishingly teach the three," the commentary states:
The following accords with the present reality.
There are two parts:

first, the explanation of extinction through the teaching of the Dharma and the announcement of the transformation-body as the truth; second, the combined explanation of extinction, the transformation-body, and the announcement of the truth.
This is the first.
This is divided into two parts:
first, explaining that [the state of the two vehicles] is not ultimate; second, explaining the intention of the two vehicles.
Regarding the statement, "What you have done is not yet accomplished," the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:

“Because Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas have not exhausted the dharmas of further birth, they possess birth; because their holy life (brahmacarya) is incomplete, it is not pure; because their task is not finalized, there remains that which must be done; because they have not crossed over to the other shore, there remains that which must be abandoned; and because they have not abandoned [these], they remain far from the realm of Nirvana.”
"What has not yet been accomplished must indeed be accomplished; this refers to the Noble Truth of the Path.
This is because there still remains the wisdom of the Truth of the Path—the emptiness of phenomena—which is that which ought to be accomplished."
By citing this, the rest should also be understood as subjects for training.

Your holy life has been established and you possess the knowledge of the Truth of Cessation; you have realized the stage of Nirvana with remainder and are close to the Buddha’s wisdom, yet what you have attained is not ultimate.

Because the remaining aspects of the holy life have not been accomplished, they are not pure; that is to say, the cognitive obscurations have not yet been extinguished and non-abiding nirvāṇa has not yet been attained. Therefore, one should investigate and deliberate upon suffering and its origin.
Since these two types of wisdom are likewise not ultimate, the nirvāṇa attained through them is not truly real.
This being so, how much more so the initial teaching of the Two Vehicles, which was intended merely as the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means.
The Sūtra says: "Just as that guide [reaches the destination], so too do I manifest transformations.
The commentary states:
This explains, in combination, the cessation of transformations and the proclamation of the truth.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “At that time, the World-Honored One arrived” up to “it rained down again those that were fresh and fine,” the commentary states:
the following forty-nine and a half verses.
This is divided into two parts:
the first thirty and a half verses praise the previously mentioned past causes, which led [beings] to abandon the Great Vehicle and resort to the Small;

the nineteen verses concerning the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū praise the manifestation of the present fruit, which enables them to know how to relinquish the provisional and take up the real, as illustrated by the parable of the conjured city.
The initial section further divides into two parts:
first, twenty-eight and a half verses on past causes and conditions; second, the final two verses concluding with an admonition not to fear.
The first part further divides into two sub-sections:
The first twenty-seven and a half verses summarize the events concerning the Buddha’s own life, while the final verse summarizes the events concerning his disciples.
Regarding the initial prose section, there are two parts:
first, an account of the duration since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; second, the actual clarification of those events.
Now we shall only versify the latter portion, as the former has already been versified.
Regarding that subject matter, there are four sections in the prose; here it is likewise so:

first, four verses clarify the Buddha’s lifespan and his attainment of enlightenment; second, thirteen verses describe the turning of the wheel of the true Dharma; third, nine and a half verses concern the succession of the lamp by his son; and fourth, the final verse brings the assembly together with the present Buddha.
The beginning and middle sections consist of two parts:
the first three verses concern the non-manifestation of the Dharma, while the final verse clarifies the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.
The Buddha’s lifespan is not versified.
The beginning and middle sections further consist of two parts:
the first verse describes the non-manifestation of the Dharma, while the latter two verses describe offerings of flowers and music.
These constitute the two textual passages; they do not include a verse on the arrangement of seats.
In the prose version, there is only the Brahmā Heaven raining flowers; here, the eight classes of beings are added.
Regarding the scripture’s passage, “After ten intermediate kalpas had passed, their hearts were filled with leaping joy,” the commentary says:
This clarifies the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment.
Regarding the passage in the sutra from "The sixteen sons of that Buddha" to "shaking all things," the commentary says:
The second section below consists of thirteen verses on the Turning of the Wheel of the True Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
It has two parts:
the first eight verses are the request, and the latter five verses are the actual turning.
The request consists of two parts:
the first three verses consist of sixteen sub-requests, which do not include offerings;
the latter five verses consist of the requests of the various Brahmā kings.
This is the first [section].
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “In the various worlds of the eastern direction... until he accepted the invitation and sat silently,” the commentary says:
The following five verses record the invitation by the Brahmā King;
the first three verses concern the eastern direction, while the latter two concern the remaining directions.
This is the first [verse].
The textual passage also consists of four parts, which may be understood by referring to the preceding section.
Regarding the Sūtra’s statement, “In the three directions and the four intermediate points... up to turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma,” the commentary says:
The remaining sections are invitations from other regions.
Regarding the passage in the Sūtra from “The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom” to “you all should know,” the commentary says:
The five verses below constitute the actual exposition,
which is twofold:
the first two verses grant permission for the formal teaching, and the latter three verses describe the benefits obtained by sentient beings.
This is the first [section].

Regarding the statement, "From ignorance up to old age and death, all arise conditioned by birth," this explains the meaning of the prose passage: ignorance conditions formations (*saṃskāra*), formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so on, up to birth conditioning old age and death.
This term "arising" (*jāti*) does not refer to the link of arising itself, but rather to that which causes arising to arise.

This term "existence" (*bhava*) does not refer to the link of existence itself, but to the existence of non-existence; that is to say, just as the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) exists because it arises through the condition of the link of ignorance (*avidyā*), the essence of the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) exists because it arises through the condition of the preceding link of volitional formations, and so on, up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), which exist because they arise through the condition of the preceding link of birth (*jāti*).
They do not arise without cause or from an unequal cause, because they all arise from conditions.

This demonstrates that ignorance exists as the condition capable of producing old age and death; because this cyclic progression is inexhaustible, it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
The Sūtra states: "When this Dharma is proclaimed, one cannot reach its limit.
The commentary says:
This refers to sentient beings attaining benefit.
The first verse praises the First Assembly, the next praises the Second Assembly, and the final one praises the Third and Fourth Assemblies.
The character "姟" (hài) is pronounced with the initial *gǔ* and the final *āi*; it denotes a numerical value.
The *Fengsu Tong* states: "Ten thousand is called a wan; one hundred thousand is called a yi; one billion is called a zhao; ten billion is called a jing; and one hundred billion is called a hai."
"Yòu dà shù" (猶大數) refers to the previously mentioned six million *billion* (*nayuta*) *trillions* (*koṭi*).
A *nayuta* is a *hài* (姟). The scripture states:
"At that time, the sixteen princes attained the foremost purity of the wisdom-eye."
The commentary states:
The third section below continues the transmission of the lamp.
There are five parts in the prose narrative, and four are contained herein:

The commentary says: This concludes the preceding section. Regarding the "Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies upon the Five Hundred Disciples," there is a threefold analysis: [1] the title; [2] the introductory summary; and [3] the detailed exposition. The first, the title, is as follows: "The Chapter on the Bestowal of Prophecies upon the Five Hundred Disciples. As for the second, the introductory summary: [text follows].
First, the purpose of its arrival; second, the explanation of its title; third, the resolution of difficulties.
Regarding the fourfold purpose of its arrival:

first, those of superior faculties attain prediction upon hearing the Dharma once; those of middling faculties receive prediction upon hearing the Dharma twice; now, as those of inferior faculties have been able to achieve awakening and understanding after hearing the Dharma three times, this chapter has therefore arrived.

Second, the Treatise states: "In order to eliminate the seven kinds of overweening pride (*abhimāna*) found among sentient beings who possess the nature of the seven types of afflictions, the fifth—those of indeterminate character who produce false understandings and give rise to overweening pride regarding inferior states of mind—for their sake, the parable of the tied jewel is taught."

This means that those with distracted minds truly lack meditative concentration; although they possessed roots of goodness in the Mahāyāna in the past, they were unaware of them. Not seeking the Mahāyāna, they conceived false notions regarding inferior states of mind, taking them to be the supreme vehicle. To counteract this, the parable of the tied jewel is taught.
Therefore, the treatise further states: "The fifth person demonstrates past roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) so that they may be reminded of the teaching and enter into samādhi.

These are those in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who have not yet attained a concentrated mind; they cling to the path of the two vehicles as ultimate and do not know their past Mahāyāna roots of goodness. Now, they are made to enter samādhi and remember those Mahāyāna roots of goodness from that time, like one who has fallen asleep after drinking wine with a precious jewel tied securely to them. For this reason, this chapter follows."
Third, among the ten unsurpassed [teachings], this fourth is the unsurpassed [teaching] that brings about understanding; it employs the parable of the tied jewel.

This means that by recounting past conditions, it causes [beings] to give rise to awakening and understanding, so that they may know there exists the wondrous jewel of the roots of goodness of the Mahāyāna; therefore, this chapter follows.
This meaning is incomplete.
Fourth, the commentary explains that the presentation of the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) is manifested in six locations:
first, the individual prophecy, which refers to Śāriputra and the four great śrāvakas.

Second, regarding the simultaneous bestowal of predictions: Pūrṇa and the others—five hundred and twelve hundred [monks]—shared a single name unknown to the multitude; because they were all granted predictions at the same time, this chapter follows.

However, Pūrṇa’s name is Dharmaprabhāsa, while the others are named Samantaprabhāsa; because the meaning of "prabhāsa" (illumination) is identical and because many share the same name, this is called a "common prediction.
To explain the characters: the pronunciation of "shòu" (to receive/accept) is zhí yǒu (植酉); according to the *Yùpiān*, it means "to contain," "to lead," or "to obtain."
"Five hundred" refers to the number; "disciples" refers to the persons; and "receiving a prediction" (vyākaraṇa) refers to the event. These names are derived from these three factors.
Because five hundred disciples received and accepted the Buddha’s prediction, this recording of them is termed "receiving a prediction."
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound).
To resolve the objection, one asks:

Question: Among the ten unsurpassed [teachings] and the seven similes, all speak of "tying a precious jewel. Why is this not taken as the title, instead of using "receiving the prediction" (vyākaraṇa) as the designation?

Answer: When the faculties have matured and the aspiration for enlightenment is generated, one immediately receives the prediction; it is only subsequently that the simile of tying the precious jewel is explained.
It is named "Receiving the Prediction" (vyākaraṇa) because it is designated from its very beginning.
Question:

Since those of superior faculties and others all received [the teaching] prior to the prediction, for what reason do the five hundred receive realization only after the prediction—specifically, that the binding of the jewel is the realization of the five hundred disciples?
Answer: Those of superior and middling faculties do not depend upon receiving a prediction; they attain understanding immediately upon hearing the teaching.
Those of inferior faculties, whose natures are inherently slow, only give rise to a sense of joy after receiving the prediction.
Since the joyful mind has already been aroused, one is now able to express one's realization;
therefore, this differs from the two previous instances of comprehension.

Furthermore, although the lower-capacity Subhūti had already realized the truth prior to this, he restated his original intent after the records for the five hundred of the lowest grade were concluded, because his realization was profound and significant—he did not realize it for the first time at this specific moment, as he had already realized it previously.
Question:
Within this chapter, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra and his twelve hundred companions all received their predictions; why then are only five hundred specifically recorded by name? Answer:
There are four interpretations:
first, it is said that the five hundred were present in the assembly and received their predictions in person, whereas the twelve hundred were not in the assembly and did not receive them in person.
The second [interpretation] states that five hundred buddhas personally conferred predictions upon them, while for the twelve hundred people, the Buddha caused them to be recorded through verses.

The third [interpretation] states that for the five hundred people, the Buddha gave individual predictions—meaning he specifically described their characteristics in terms such as "successive prediction" (*anupūrvavyākaraṇa*) and so forth;
whereas for the twelve hundred people, the Buddha gave only a general prediction without specifically manifesting their individual characteristics.
Fourth, it is said that because these five hundred people were capable of generating understanding and realization, the parable of the tied jewel was taught;
whereas the twelve hundred others had no distinct realization, and since Pūrṇa alone was deficient in this regard, it was not taught to him.
Therefore, the chapter is titled simply "Five Hundred" because it represents a complete number; it is not titled after numbers such as "One Thousand Two Hundred," as those figures are incomplete.
The sutra says: "At that time, Pūrṇa [attained] the power of supernatural penetrations."
The commentary states:
This chapter’s main text is divided into three parts.
Regarding the four sections of the third cycle of teaching, those above were spoken by the Buddha; therefore, there are three [sections] below:

First, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra receives understanding through his mental reflection; next, from "At that time the Buddha said" onwards, the World-Honored One speaks to confirm and describe it; finally, from "The bhikṣus and Pūrṇa [have also served] the seven Buddhas" onwards, he formally bestows the prophecy.
One person acts as the leader, and the same principle applies to the rest; this is because by briefly citing one corner, the other three corners are understood.
The first section has two parts:
first, clarifying the understanding and reverent respect; second, clarifying the mental recitation of that understanding.
The initial passage is further divided into two parts:
first, clarifying what is received; second, clarifying reverent devotion.
This is the former.
There are four aspects of what is governed:
first, governing the teaching of the Dharma; proximately, governing the transformation city and the place of treasure;
and distantly, governing the section from the "Expedient Means" chapter downward, wherein the provisional comes first and the real follows.

Second is the reception of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). The proximate reception refers to the end of the "Chapter on Prediction," which states: "My disciples, endowed with majestic virtue, numbering five hundred, shall all receive predictions that in a future age they will all attain Buddhahood.
The remote reception refers to the predictions bestowed upon Śāriputra and those below him.

The three chapters lead [us] back to past causes and conditions: the *Upāya-paryāya* chapter refers to the immediate past, citing the sixteen princes as lay followers (*upāsaka*) who "in life after life have already received transformation from the Buddha," while the *Parable* chapter speaks of the distant past, saying, "In the past, I taught you to set your will upon the Buddha-way."

The fourth category concerns the mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā-abhijñā*). This includes, in its proximate sense, the establishment of the "provisional city" (*nirmita-nagara*) described in the preceding chapter; this refers to the supernormal power of the Great Buddha who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten *kalpas*, shook the ten directions, emitted light that shone afar throughout the ten directions, and was joined by Brahma Kings who came to behold the splendor—all such matters.

In its remote sense, it includes Śākyamuni’s initial gathering of the assembly, the shaking of the earth, the raining of flowers, and the emission of light shining afar, as well as the passage in the "Expedient Means" (*Upāya-paryāya*) chapter which says: "While I was reflecting thus, a Brahma voice consoled me, saying, 'Excellent, Śākyamuni! All these are the supernormal powers of the Buddhas.
Regarding the passage from "attaining what they had never before experienced" to "not for a moment averting their eyes," the commentary states:
This clarifies reverent devotion.

There are eight [actions]: first, attaining a rare dharma; second, purification of the mind; third, leaping for joy; fourth, rising from one's seat; fifth, approaching the Buddha; sixth, prostrating at his feet; seventh, withdrawing to stand aside; eighth, gazing up with reverence.

This clarifies the mental reflection and understanding.

Regarding the passage from "At that time the Buddha said" to "Maitrāyaṇīputra,

This is the third major section of the third cycle below, wherein the World-Honored One speaks to provide a seal of approval and a summary.
There are three parts:
first, asking whether the assembly has seen it; second, praising his present virtues starting from "I have always praised him"; and third, discussing his past virtues starting from "Do not say this."
This is the first point.
"Seeing" has the meaning of consciousness; it is not that which is invisible to the eyes of the multitude, but rather that the mind does not recognize the nature of one's virtuous conduct.
Furthermore, "seeing" has the meaning of looking: do you see him standing before you right now?

Furthermore, although many may have seen him, they may not necessarily have kept it in mind; now, wishing to speak of his virtuous conduct, he asks whether they have seen him, desiring that sentient beings gaze upon and observe his virtuous conduct with focused attention, and for this reason he asks, "Have you seen him?"
The Sūtra says: “I constantly extol his various supreme merits.
The commentary states:
This below praises his present virtues.
There are two parts:
first, praising the person; second, praising his virtues.
There are two aspects to praising his virtues:
The first part is general and the latter part is specific.
This praises the person and offers a general praise of their virtues.
The sutra states: "Diligently protecting and upholding [the Dharma]... up to the eloquence of discourse."
The commentary says:
This is a specific praise of his virtues.
There are five [aspects]:

First, assisting in the proclamation of the True Dharma; second, being able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the fourfold assembly; third, being able to explain the Buddha-dharma; fourth, benefiting those who practice together; and fifth, possessing lofty and profound eloquence.
"Abundant" (*rào*) means much.
"Plentiful" (*fēng*) means thick, increased, or surplus.
The Sūtra says: "Do not say that [this]... is also the most supreme."
The commentary says:
The following discusses past virtues.
There are ten [sections], of which there are two here:
First, protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma, acting as a guardian of the city of the Dharma by upholding and embracing the True Dharma;
second, becoming a superior person.
As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, regarding all Buddhas... until there is no doubt."
The commentary states:
This [wisdom] possesses four virtues.
First, it understands the two kinds of emptiness, because it contemplates existence through the lens of emptiness.
Second, they attain the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), because they abide on the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Third, they constantly and carefully proclaim the teachings, because they accord with what has been realized and are free from the referents of verbal expression.
Fourth, they are free from doubt, because both doubts regarding principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*) have been completely exhausted.
The Sūtra states: "Endowed with the qualities of a bodhisattva... up to a hundred thousand sentient beings.
The commentary says:
This possesses three virtues.
First, they possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), because they perform great deeds within the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*);
second, they cultivate pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), because they constantly maintain the threefold bodhisattva vows;
third, they conceal their great benefit while acting for the welfare of sentient beings through the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, he transforms immeasurable [beings]... until he teaches and transforms sentient beings.
The commentary states:
This refers to one virtue herein.

Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "The One Vehicle is taught for the sake of transformation. This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas to guide those of a similar kind and cause them to resolve upon the Great Mind.
This is also what the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Having indulged in the wine of samādhi for many kalpas, one awakens from that intoxication and only then gives rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*).

I have exhorted other śrāvakas, saying: 'I have entered parinirvāṇa through the nirvāṇa without remainder of the śrāvaka vehicle countless hundreds of times; because that is not true extinction, I have arisen from it and now, once again, give rise to the Great Mind.'"
"Why do you still abide in the Lesser Vehicle now?
Such meanings are as explained previously in the Chapter on the One Vehicle.
This virtue has two aspects:
First, the practice of benefiting others, which involves transforming others so that they may establish themselves in unsurpassed enlightenment;
second, the practice of benefiting oneself through the very act of benefiting others, whereby one constantly performs the Buddha-work in order to purify the buddha-fields.
The Sūtra states: “The bhikṣus who have arrived are likewise foremost.
The commentary says:
This concludes the fourth major section of the third cycle, which is specifically for the purpose of bestowing predictions of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
There are two parts:
first, the bestowal of the prediction upon Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra; second, the bestowal of the predictions upon the five hundred disciples.
Within the first prediction, there are again two sections.
First, the causes are predicted, and subsequently, the results are predicted.
There are six types of predictions regarding causes; this is the first, predicting the attainment of the status of a supreme person.
"The Seven Buddhas" refers to the seven Buddhas of the past.
In the preceding kalpa there were three Buddhas, namely Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, and Viśvabhū Buddha.
In the Bhadrakalpa there are four, namely Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha.
The meanings concerning the Bhadrakalpa and so forth are all as explained in the *Commentary on Maitreya’s Ascent*.
This constitutes the general presentation of the seven Buddhas of the past.
The phrase "now, in my [time]" refers to the specific presentation of the present.
The Sūtra says: "And they shall all protect and uphold [this] until reaching supreme enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
The commentary states:
This contains two types of prophecies (vyākaraṇa).
First, protecting and assisting in the proclamation of the Dharma; second, transforming others to establish them in Bodhi.
As the Sūtra says: "For the sake of purifying the Buddha-land... up to the path of the Bodhisattva.
The commentary states:
There are three records concerning this:
first, constant diligence; second, benefiting sentient beings; and third, being endowed with the bodhisattva path.
The sutra states: "Passing through immeasurable [eons] until reaching the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
The commentary states:
This is the record of the lower fruits.
There are six; these are their names and titles.
Because one clearly understands the meaning of the Dharma,
it is called "Dharma-illumination" (dharmāloka). Regarding the sutra passage, "That Buddha [is] filled therein," the commentary says:
Next is the second section on the characteristics of the land.
It has two parts:
first, the exposition; second, the conclusion.
Manifestation has six aspects; herein there are two:
first, breadth and narrowness; second, characteristics.
There are three types of characteristics:
First, the jeweled ground;
second, the level ground.
Regarding "ling" (陵), the *Yupian* states: "A great mound; furthermore, it refers to hills, mounds, and tombs."
"Guan" (㵎) is the name of a watercourse.
A body of water four feet wide and deep is called a "gou" (溝).
"He" (壑) refers to a valley, a depth, a pit, an emptiness, or a cavernous chamber.
The Third Terrace Pavilion.
The Sūtra says: "The palaces of the various devas extend to where there is no sexual desire.
The commentary states:
Among these, there is one [type of existence] that possesses goodness and lacks evil.
There are four [characteristics]: first, proximity to the heavens; second, mutual visibility; third, the absence of women of the evil realms; and fourth, desireless birth by transformation.
The Sūtra says: "Having attained great supernormal powers, they arrive and adorn themselves.
The commentary states:
Herein, too, there is one [aspect], namely the characteristics of humans and devas.

There are seven: first, the attainment of supernatural powers; second, bodily radiance; third, the ability to fly; fourth, firm resolve; fifth, diligence; sixth, wisdom; and seventh, the primary and secondary marks of physical excellence.
The Sūtra says: "The sentient beings of that land... subsist on the food of meditative joy.
The Commentary states:
This refers to only one [of the four nutriments], namely, the sustenance of food (*āhāra*).
This explains two types of sustenance; the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* speaks of two: being sustained by the joy and bliss of the flavor of the vast Dharma.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "Having partaken of the deathless Dharma, one drinks again the flavor of liberation."
Other sūtras speak of four types: edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), contact (sparśa), volition (manas-karma), and consciousness (vijñāna).
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks of four:
first, impure; second, pure; third, both pure and impure; and fourth, the sustenance that serves as the basis for manifestation.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* explains nine kinds of nutriment (*āhāra*):
four are mundane nutriments, and five are supramundane nutriments.
What are the four kinds of mundane nutriment?
These are the food of morsels, the food of contact, the food of volition, and the food of consciousness.
Their characteristics have been explained in detail.
What are the five kinds of supramundane food?
First is the food of dhyāna; second is the food of aspiration; third is the food of mindfulness; fourth is the food of the eight liberations; and fifth is the food of joy.
One should always be single-mindedly intent on abandoning these four kinds of worldly food and seeking these five kinds of supramundane food.
Untainted dharmas shatter tainted states, yet they are not the nutriment of the tainted;
tainted dharmas oppose and harm the untainted, yet they are not the nutriment of the untainted.
In reality, each is called a nutriment.
That which serves as a temporary support may be provisionally called "food," but ultimately it is not.

This [text], along with the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, speaks only of untainted (*anāsrava*) food and not tainted (*sāsrava*) food; other sources speak of the four types of food as being exclusively tainted food and not untainted food.
The *Āgamas* speak of nine [types of nutriment], which encompass both kinds of food.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* speaks of four, which distinguish food based on persons rather than as dharmic food.
The joy and bliss born from the flavor of the Dharma that differs from the stage of Buddhahood is precisely this "Dharma-joy."

This is based on the initial attainment, which occurs only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); since it pertains to the desire realm and takes the teachings as its object, it is said that "joy is the nutriment.
However, in subsequent times, it also extends to the six consciousnesses; because it is present throughout the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), both joy and pleasure (*sukha*) are opened up.
This is collectively termed "joy" (*prīti*), because it shares the same quality of mental satisfaction;
whereas that [previous case] refers only to external conditions and does not mention the joy of dhyāna, the joy of dhyāna being precisely the food of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).

This [present case], however, speaks generally of internal conditions and thus includes the joy of dhyāna; based on its initial attainment, which occurs solely within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is designated simply as "joy-food."

In that *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, two superior types of food—both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)—are posited as sustenance.
